name: Investigative Planning and Design
what: This subtopic covers how to structure and document a scientific investigation using a logbook. It includes how to write each section of the logbook — from the title and introduction through to the method — and what level of detail is required for each.
why: A well-kept logbook is required for VCE assessment and authenticates that primary data was collected by the investigator. Clear documentation also allows others to repeat or reproduce your investigation, which is essential for valid scientific practice.

items.title: I can explain the purpose of a logbook in a scientific investigation
items.what: A logbook is a dated, handwritten record of all stages of an investigation — from planning through to results and reflections. It authenticates primary data by showing it was recorded firsthand by the investigator.
items.why: VCE requires students to maintain a logbook for all practical activities in Units 1–4. A physical logbook reduces the likelihood of tampering with results and provides verifiable evidence of authentic data collection.
items.example: A student records the date, the title of their investigation, their aim, hypothesis, method and results table all in their logbook before conducting the experiment. Each entry is dated so the sequence of work can be verified.

items.title: I can write a clear and specific title for a scientific investigation
items.what: A title states the research question under investigation and should reference both the independent variable (what is being changed) and the dependent variable (what is being measured).
items.why: A specific title immediately communicates the scope of the investigation to any reader and distinguishes a focused, single-variable exploration from a vague or overly broad question.
items.example: A weak title: 'Determine the effect of a catalyst on the rate of a chemical reaction.' A stronger title: 'Does the addition of invertase result in an increased rate of glucose production through its function as a catalyst on the hydrolysis of sucrose?'

items.title: I can write an introduction that explains the chemical context of an investigation
items.what: The introduction provides a detailed but concise explanation of the chemistry behind the investigation. It includes relevant chemical equations, key concepts and definitions, and links the background theory to the aim and hypothesis.
items.why: Examiners assess whether students understand the chemistry underpinning their investigation, not just the procedure. A strong introduction demonstrates that the experimental design is grounded in scientific theory.
items.example: In an invertase investigation, the introduction would explain that invertase is an enzyme that catalyses the hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose, lowering activation energy. It would include the equation: C12H22O11(aq) + H2O(l) → C6H12O6(aq) + C6H12O6(aq).

items.title: I can write a method with sufficient detail for the investigation to be repeated
items.what: A method is a series of clearly numbered steps that describes exactly how the investigation was conducted, including specific quantities, concentrations, equipment, timepoints and any control conditions.
items.why: A method that lacks specific quantities or equipment cannot be repeated by other investigators, which means the investigation cannot be confirmed as reproducible. VCE assessment requires methods detailed enough for full reproducibility.
items.example: A weak method step: 'Add enzyme to the test tube.' A stronger step: 'Add 3.00 mL of 5.0 x 10^-2 mg mL^-1 invertase solution to the test tube containing 3.00 mL of 50.0 mg mL^-1 sucrose solution pre-incubated at 40.0°C.'

items.title: I can distinguish between primary data and secondary data
items.what: Primary data is collected firsthand by the investigator through experiments, observations, fieldwork or surveys. Secondary data is existing data collected by someone else, such as published journal articles, books or websites.
items.why: Understanding this distinction matters for logbook authentication and for correctly citing sources. VCE investigations require students to generate their own primary data, but the introduction often draws on secondary sources to establish context.
items.example: The glucose concentration readings a student records from their own titration experiment are primary data. The accepted value for the specific heat capacity of water (4.18 J g^-1 °C^-1) found in a textbook is secondary data.
